sentences.text: At the 21% O2 design air, a thin material rated at 1 g between 21.0% and 24.9% O2 passes the 1-g test but could burn in reduced gravity at the largest loss measured.
The biggest gap is that PSI's ISS solid-material tables stop at 22.2% O2, and its 26-40% O2 band holds 84 conditions with 0 solid-material flames.
A materials engineer should carry the measured margin loss, mean -2.62 points and worst -3.9 points, into any thin-material 1-g rating, and should test above 22.2% O2.
The ISS design air is well covered: FLEX measured burning at 21.0% O2 and 14.7 psia, the 21% design point itself.
The biggest gap is that the ISS solid-material tables stop at 22.2% O2, and the 26-40% O2 band has 0 solid-material flames in 84 conditions.
Mission planners should apply the -3.9-point worst-case margin loss to any 1-g rating, and fund solid-material tests above 22.2% O2 before relying on those ratings.
At the 30% O2 design air, a thin material rated at 1 g between 30.0% and 33.9% O2 passes the 1-g test but could burn in reduced gravity at the largest loss measured.
The biggest gap is that PSI's solid-material tables stop at 22.2% O2 against a 30% design air, and PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data.
Mission planners should review the 8 LUCI records at 0.167 g in the verified literature, and commission combustion tests at lunar gravity and 30% O2.
At 30% O2 and 0.38 g, a thin material rated at 1 g between 30.0% and 33.9% O2 passes the 1-g test but could burn in reduced gravity at the largest loss measured.
The biggest gap is that the verified partial-gravity records sit at 0.167 g, not at Mars's 0.38 g, and PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data.
Materials engineers should carry the largest measured margin loss, -3.9 points, into 1-g ratings, and planners should test thin materials at 0.38 g and 30% O2.
At 34% O2 and 8.2 psia, a thin material rated at 1 g between 34.0% and 37.9% O2 passes the 1-g test but could burn in reduced gravity at the largest loss measured.
The biggest gap is that PSI's solid-material tables stop at 22.2% O2 and PSI holds no partial-gravity data, while this rover is designed for 34% O2 at 0.166 g.
Planners should use the closest in-orbit point, ACME CFI-G at 34.1% O2 and 7.3 psia, as a reference, and carry the -3.9-point margin loss into any 1-g rating.
BRE tests whether turning off ventilation, a standard spacecraft firefighting step, may leave fires burning at elevated oxygen, which matters for crew response in a higher-oxygen cabin.
Its 3 tabulated conditions span 21.0% to 34.0% O2 and reach the 30% Moon air, but table pressures are not listed, so reduced-pressure behavior is not tabulated.
Use its ventilation-off result as a test case for Moon-base suppression procedures; no verified literature record names BRE yet, so its flight results are the only source.
BASS asks whether NASA's 1-g upward-burn screening test is really worst case for space, which goes to how thin materials are cleared for crewed cabins.
BASS reports extinction at gravity 0 with a 1 cm/s extinction flow for SIBAL fabric, but oxygen and pressure are not tabulated, so it cannot be placed in 30% O2 air.
Use its 2.55 mm/s and 1.21 mm/s spread rates for SIBAL fabric at gravity 0 as baseline inputs for a 30% O2 cabin test, rather than as lunar results.
BASS-II maps when flames spread or go out as oxygen falls from about 22% to about 14%, which gives thresholds that matter for crewed fire response at lower oxygen.
Its 129 tabulated conditions reach 22.2% O2, and PMMA flame spread was not observed below 16.4% O2 at gravity 0, but the 30% Moon air and partial gravity are not in its data.
Use its 16.1% and 13.3% PMMA extinction values, the second from a linear-fit intercept, to bound how much threshold depends on analysis method before applying either to lunar air.
FLEX maps the lowest oxygen that sustains burning and how CO2 and helium suppress flames, which is relevant to cabin suppression planning.
Its 274 tabulated conditions span 12.0% to 34.0% O2 and 0.69 to 3.05 atm, which covers 30% O2 air, but its fuels are methanol and heptane, not solid materials.
Use its methanol flammability limits of 12% and 13% at gravity 0.0 as a benchmark for a lunar-air test plan, and add solid-material and partial-gravity cases.
Saffire-II compares microgravity burn length with 1-g behavior for spacecraft materials burned in an empty Cygnus, a cabin-scale comparison relevant to crew fire planning.
Its 9 tabulated conditions sit at 21.5% to 22.1% O2, derived from CO2 production, so none reach the 30% Moon air.
Use its 2.1 mm/s and 2.6 mm/s cotton-fiberglass spread rates, measured at gravity 0 in an empty Cygnus, as a check on fabric models before any Moon-base test.
BASS flame-spread modeling provides a predictive model of concurrent flame spread for spacecraft materials, built from BASS videos, which could extend those tests to untested conditions.
It has 0 tabulated conditions and inherits its oxygen and pressure from BASS and BASS-II, so it cannot establish 30% O2 or partial-gravity behavior on its own.
Use the model to screen concurrent-flow cases, then check its predictions against measured data at 30% O2 before any Moon-base use.
Saffire-I measured flame growth, heat and O2/CO2 for a meter-long fabric sheet at realistic spacecraft scale, so its data bear directly on crew fire response.
Its 2 tabulated conditions sit at 21.5% O2 with pressure not tabulated, so its data do not reach the 30% Moon air.
Use its 40 mm concurrent and 24 mm opposed flame lengths at gravity 0 as cabin-scale reference values for flame-length checks, noting they are at 21.5% O2.
Saffire-III repeats the meter-scale fabric fire at 30 cm/s airflow, giving a flow-speed comparison point against Saffire-I.
Its oxygen and pressure are not tabulated and it has 0 tabulated conditions with O2, so its 2.3 mm/s spread and 8 s ignition cannot be placed in lunar air.
Use its 2.3 mm/s and 0.98 mm/s spread results as cabin-scale fabric checks, keeping their gravity and oxygen limits in view.
FLEX-2 extends FLEX to real-fuel surrogates and mixtures under slow forced flow, a condition that matters for ventilated cabins.
Its 20 tabulated conditions span 17.0% to 30.0% O2 and 0.5 to 3.0 atm, reaching the 30% Moon air at its upper edge, with 0 verified literature records naming it.
Use its 0.1 to 5 cm/s droplet-translation cases to test whether forced flow changes extinction at the 30.0% O2 upper edge of its table.
SAME measured smoke particle sizes from overheated spacecraft materials on ISS and how real smoke detectors responded, the core dataset for spacecraft smoke detection.
It does not tabulate oxygen or pressure, so its particle sizes cannot be placed in 30% O2 or reduced-pressure Moon air.
Use its 0.047 µm unaged and 0.102 µm aged Kapton particle sizes to compare unaged and aged smoke before setting detector thresholds for a lunar cabin.
SAME-R re-flew SAME with new materials, hotter heating and a new instrument to fix contamination problems and broaden smoke-detection data.
Oxygen and pressure are both unknown in its table, and its 1-8.1 cm/s inlet velocity cannot be tied to 30% O2 or reduced-pressure Moon air.
Use it as a second detector-response set beside SAME, and record oxygen and pressure in any repeat run before using it for lunar design.
Flame Design maps when flames make soot and when they go out across a wide oxygen and pressure range, which bears on fire behavior in oxygen-rich cabin air.
Its 316 tabulated conditions span 19.8% to 85.0% O2 and 0.43 to 3.0 atm, which covers 30% O2 air, but its fuels are ethylene and methane, not solid materials.
Use the 870 s steady-flame record and the 1000 K model peak temperature to bracket flame duration and temperature cases in a lunar test plan.
CFI-G shows cool flames at 500 to 1000 K that are hard to see yet still burning, and can jump back to hot flames, which matters for detection and re-ignition.
Its 333 tabulated conditions span 12.0% to 85.0% O2 and 0.49 to 3.27 atm, so 30% Moon air falls inside the table, though its fuels are ethane, propane, n-butane and n-pentane.
Use its ethane flammability limit of 0.317 slpm and extinction flow of 0.051 slpm at gravity 0 as gas-phase benchmarks for lunar tests.
The CFD shows how small drafts or heat sources keep cool flames alive or extinguish them, which matters for airflow changes in a habitat.
It has 0 tabulated conditions and takes its oxygen from FLEX, so it cannot establish behavior at 30% O2 or under partial gravity on its own.
Use its imposed-convection sweeps to set airflow limits for cool-flame tests, then validate them with measured data at 30% O2.
SPICE located the smoke point, where a flame starts releasing soot, for 526 flames in space, which indicates how smoky an accidental fire would be.
Its coflow air is 21% O2 and pressure is not tabulated, so its smoke points cannot be placed in 30% O2 or reduced-pressure Moon air.
Use its propylene and N2 flame lengths of 34.62 mm, 38.64 mm and 28.67 mm at 1.0 g as a 1 g comparison set when checking smoke-point models.
CFI studies low-temperature cool flames of jet-fuel-like droplets, which matters for understanding unexpected re-ignition and low-temperature chemistry.
Its 87 tabulated conditions cover 17.0% to 21.0% O2 only, so they end at 21.0% O2 and do not reach the 30% Moon air.
Use its 25.0 W cool-flame result for dodecane at gravity 0.0 and its 1200 K heptane model temperature as bounds in cool-flame test planning.
CLD Flame measured coflow flames from near-extinction to heavily sooting, giving soot-model inputs for fire simulations.
Its oxygen and pressure are not tabulated and it has 0 tabulated conditions, so it cannot be placed in 30% O2 or reduced-pressure Moon air.
Use it as a source of soot-model inputs for weak-coflow simulations, and collect oxygen and pressure values before applying it to a lunar base.
SPICE data analysis extracts soot temperature and concentration from existing SPICE images, comparing 0 g and 1 g to improve soot models.
It has 0 tabulated conditions and inherits its oxygen and pressure from SPICE, so it cannot place soot results in 30% O2 Moon air on its own.
Use its extracted soot temperatures to check soot-model predictions at ground conditions, and add 30% O2 and partial-gravity cases before lunar use.
s-Flame grows spherical flames of hydrogen, methane and ethylene at about 21% and 30% O2 to test detailed chemistry and radiation models.
Its 2 tabulated conditions cover 21.0% and 30.0% O2 at about 1 atm, so 30% O2 is tested only near 1 atm.
Use its ethylene extinction flows of 8 cc/s and 1 cc/s, and the methane value of 1 cc/s, as kinetic-extinction benchmarks for flow-based flame tests.
The counterflow work links FLEX's cool flames to general flammability-limit diagrams, which helps place cool-flame results across conditions.
It has 0 tabulated conditions, and its 20 atm pressure is simulated, so it cannot establish Moon-base behavior at 30% O2 by itself.
Use its counterflow strain cases to define test matrices for cool-flame limits, then run them at 30% O2 with reduced pressure.
The simulation explains why smoke particles grow differently in microgravity, which supports detector design for spacecraft smoke.
Its oxygen and pressure are not applicable, so its results cannot be placed in 30% O2 or reduced-pressure Moon air.
Use its low cross-flow velocity cases to check particle-growth assumptions in detector models before applying them to lunar cabins.
SLICE studies what keeps a flame attached to its burner or lets it lift off and blow out in microgravity, which bears on flame stability in a cabin.
It has 0 tabulated conditions and an air coflow of 21% O2, so its flame-stability results do not reach the 30% O2 Moon air.
Use its methane and ethylene fuel cases at 21% coflow as a lift-off reference, then repeat them at 30% O2 before drawing lunar conclusions.
E-FIELD uses electric fields to push flames through their ions, an artificial flow or buoyancy-like force in microgravity that could support flame-control studies.
Its oxygen and pressure are not tabulated and it has 0 tabulated conditions, so it does not show behavior at 30% O2 or reduced pressure.
Treat it as a flame-control research topic rather than a suppression input until its tables record oxygen and pressure.
DAFT showed that a commercial particle counter could be modified to work without gravity, which enabled the SAME smoke measurements.
It used a non-combustion dust surrogate with oxygen and pressure not applicable, so it says nothing about flame chemistry at 30% O2.
Use it as an instrument-feasibility reference for particle sensing in a lunar cabin, not as evidence of flame behavior.
